## Simple explanation

Cross-validation evaluates a model repeatedly on different held-out parts
of a dataset. It provides a more robust view of performance than relying
on one train-validation split.

## Technical explanation

In k-fold cross-validation, data is divided into $k$ folds. The model is
trained on $k-1$ folds and evaluated on the remaining fold, repeating
until each fold has served as validation data. The results are aggregated.
Variants such as stratified, grouped, and time-series cross-validation
respect different data structures.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Performance estimates can vary with the particular split, especially when
data is limited. Cross-validation can support model comparison and
hyperparameter selection, but must be designed to avoid leakage and match
the intended deployment setting.

## How it works

Choose a splitting strategy suited to the data, fit a fresh model on each
training fold, and compute the chosen metric on its held-out fold. Aggregate
the fold-level results, while considering their variability and the fact
that folds may not be statistically independent.

## Practical example

A small image dataset can be evaluated across several stratified folds so
each fold contains examples from both classes. If multiple images come
from the same animal or photo session, a grouped split may be more
appropriate to prevent leakage.

## Common misconceptions

- Cross-validation does not eliminate bias from unrepresentative data.
- Reusing cross-validation results for extensive model selection can
  overfit the selection process.
- Random folds are not appropriate for every dataset, especially
  time-dependent or grouped observations.
